abstract: Minor introns are rare but evolutionarily conserved introns in the human genome. Defects in minor spliceosome components have been reported to cause several human diseases. Mutations in ZRSR2 are frequently observed in myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) patients. However, the precise molecular mechanism by which these mutations cause a loss of ZRSR2 function in minor intron splicing remain elusive. In this study, we characterized the impact of MDS-causing missense mutations in ZRSR2. Most of the mutant ZRSR2 proteins we tested showed different subnuclear localization pattern from that of wild-type ZRSR2 protein. Co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) analysis revealed that UHM missense mutations disrupted the interaction between ZRSR2 and SF3B complex. We also demonstrated that ZRSR2 preferentially immunoprecipitated minor spliceosome components over major spliceosome components and it directly interacts with SF3B1. Furthermore, co-IP analysis utilizing a variety of ZRSR2 mutants revealed that mutations in the UHM and Zn2 domains significantly attenuated the interaction with SF3B complex. Finally, UHM and Zn2 mutations markedly disrupted the supporting activity of ZRSR2 for minor intron splicing. Our results indicate that disruption of the physical interaction with SF3B complex is one of the hallmarks of MDS-causing mutations of ZRSR2, which results in aberrant splicing of minor introns.
